Manchester at a glance

Manchester sits on the Merrimack River in south-central New Hampshire, about 20 miles from the Massachusetts border and 58 miles from Boston. The city is in Hillsborough County, which shares its county seat role between Manchester and Nashua, and it had 115,644 residents in 2020. Many buyers commute to Boston or Concord. Close to half of occupied homes are rented, so many sales involve tenants or an owner with several properties.

The city's 2010 Master Plan divides it into 25 neighborhoods, and assessments and house styles change a lot from one to the next.

  • West Side: Amoskeag, Rimmon Heights, Notre Dame/McGregorville, and Piscataquog/Granite Square
  • East Side: North End, Janeville/Corey Square, Hallsville, and Bakersville
  • Outer areas: Youngsville and Goffes Falls

A West Side seller and a Goffes Falls seller deal with the same Board of Assessors and Tax Collector, but the buyer pool and the age of the housing can look very different.

Hillsborough County splits its seat between two cities, so deeds for a Manchester house are recorded at the Register of Deeds on Temple Street in Nashua. Plan a trip there, or ask your title company to handle the recording, so the paperwork is not left waiting at the end of your closing week.

An older mill-city housing stock

The mills defined Manchester for a century after it incorporated as a city in 1846, so the housing stock is older than most. An older house is more likely to need work before it shows well.

  • Older roofs and chimneys take freeze and thaw cycles every year.
  • Heating systems in 1960s houses are often original or near the end of their life.
  • Homes near the Merrimack, the Piscataquog or Cohas Brook deserve a look at the basement and the flood zone status before listing.

Because a cash offer already accounts for those repairs, owners with deferred work often choose to sell as is.

Elm Street and the riverside mill buildings anchor the downtown picture, but most sellers live well away from them. If your house is far from the Amoskeag district, lead with what is special about your own block: the yard, the parking, the school bus stop, the walk to a corner store.

How Manchester property tax works

Manchester taxes follow a year that begins April 1 and ends March 31 (RSA 76:2), using the April inventory. The Board of Assessors decides the value, and the Office of the Tax Collector issues the bill.

Assessors reach value three ways: recent sales of comparable properties, replacement cost less depreciation, and, for income property such as apartments, an income approach. Dividing the levy by total assessed value gives the rate, which is the same for every owner. The state Department of Revenue Administration issues it in October or November.

Two bills arrive each year. The early June bill uses half of the previous year's rate. The late November bill uses the new rate and any assessment changes. You have 30 days from the issue date to pay. The 2025 rate is 20.24 per $1,000, up from 19.58 for 2024, and a separate Central Business Service District rate of 0.462730 applies for 2025.

When taxes go unpaid

The path from overdue tax to a city deed starts with interest, reaches a lien in about a year, and can end in a deed after two years.

StepWhat happens
InterestLate taxes accrue 8 percent a year (RSA 76:13)
Notice of ArrearageMailed roughly 30 days after each billing goes out (RSA 76:11-b)
Notice of Impending LienSent by certified mail no less than 30 days ahead of the lien (RSA 80:60)
Lien executedRate jumps to 14 percent a year (RSA 80:69), and the lien is recorded at the Registry of Deeds within 30 days
Mortgagee noticeGoes out 60 days after the lien, with a $10 fee plus any title search cost (RSA 80:67)
Tax deedPossible once two years pass after the lien, following a notice of impending deed at least 30 days before (RSA 80:76, 80:77)

A former owner or mortgagee who wants the property back after a deed must tell the city by certified mail within 30 days of the notice of intent to repurchase, and must prove they can cover back taxes, interest, costs and a 10 percent penalty on the equalized assessed value (RSA 80:89).

How to challenge your assessment

Write to the Board of Assessors with an abatement application, and make sure it is received or postmarked by March 1 following the final tax bill. Filing online is not allowed because an original signature is required, and the city charges no fee.

To qualify, you must have owned the property on April 1 of the tax year, or be otherwise aggrieved, and you must demonstrate that it was assessed out of proportion to other property in town. The Board decides by July 1. Silence by then counts as a denial.

  • Any further appeal must be filed by September 1.
  • Pick one route: the State Board of Tax and Land Appeals (written, with a fee) or Hillsborough County Superior Court, Northern District, 300 Chestnut Street, Manchester.
  • Choosing the Board of Tax and Land Appeals means you cannot also petition the Superior Court (RSA 76-B:11).

If an abatement application is still pending when you sell, mention it to the title company, because the decision changes the tax bill for your year of ownership.

Selling with taxes owed

Give the title company a heads-up at the very start. At closing, whatever tax is unpaid and any recorded lien are paid from your proceeds. The Tax Collector will provide a copy of a lien release for $10 per property plus $2 per receipt requested, by email at Taxcollector@manchesternh.gov or in person at One City Hall Plaza.

A redeemed lien is released within 30 days, and the release is mailed to the Hillsborough County Register of Deeds, 19 Temple Street, Nashua. Deeds can take 30 days or longer to reach the Assessors, which means a bill may still carry your name after closing. Send the new owner's name and address along in writing.

One more habit helps: save every tax receipt you have. When the title company asks whether a given installment was paid, a receipt answers in seconds, while a bank statement takes longer to read and explain.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Transfer tax and closing paperwork

Under the state's transfer tax, each side pays $0.75 per $100 of price, with a $20 minimum apiece for prices up to $4,000. The stamps are purchased at the register of deeds. Two declarations, CD-57-P for the purchaser and CD-57-S for the seller, plus the PA-34 inventory, are due to the state within 30 days of the deed being recorded.

What buyers will ask about a Manchester house

Neighborhood matters here. A buyer looking at the West Side, the East Side or Goffes Falls will have different expectations for age and condition. Know the age of the roof and heating system, any history of a wet basement, and whether the house sits near the river or the brook. A seller who answers those questions before they are asked usually keeps the deal on track.

The interstates, the Everett Turnpike and the regional airport put many Manchester houses within easy reach of Boston, so mention the nearest on-ramp. A West Side buyer, an East Side buyer and a Goffes Falls buyer each weigh different things, and the best listing language speaks to the actual street, not the city as a whole.

Landlords selling in Manchester

With about half of occupied homes rented, many Manchester sellers are landlords. With tenants in place, pull together the leases, deposit records and rent roll before you speak with a buyer. Find out whether the building is near the river, the Piscataquog or Cohas Brook, since flood status is a common question. A cash buyer can take over a tenant-occupied building as is, but the lease terms still decide how quickly the buyer can use the property.

Landlords should also tell the title company whether the property sits in the Central Business Service District, since that district carries its own added rate.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

When is Manchester property tax due?

Each bill is due 30 days after issue. One is mailed in early June and the other in late November, for a tax year that runs April 1 to March 31.

What is the interest rate on late Manchester property tax?

8 percent per year on unpaid taxes under RSA 76:13. Once a tax lien is executed, interest on the lien is 14 percent per year under RSA 80:69.

Can I sell my Manchester house if there is a tax lien on it?

Yes. The lien is paid from the sale proceeds and released after payment, and a full redemption leads to a release within 30 days. Ask the Tax Collector for the current payoff before closing.

Who pays the New Hampshire transfer tax when a house sells?

Both. The buyer and the seller each pay $0.75 per $100 of the price, though transfers by will or intestate succession are exempt.

Where do I appeal a Manchester assessment after the Board of Assessors denies it?

File by September 1 with either the State Board of Tax and Land Appeals or Hillsborough County Superior Court, Northern District. You pick one, and choosing the state board waives the court option.

Nashua at a glance

Nashua is a city in southern New Hampshire on the Massachusetts line, in southeastern Hillsborough County. It shares the county seat role with Manchester. The 2020 count was 91,322 residents, and there were 39,663 housing units, 3.6 percent of them vacant. The Merrimack River forms the eastern boundary and the Nashua River roughly cuts the city in two.

Buyers and sellers use neighborhood names more than the official ward map:

  • Downtown, centered on Main Street and the Nashua River
  • French Hill in the north
  • The Tree Streets neighborhood near downtown
  • The Amherst Street corridor (Route 101A) in the northwest
  • South Nashua along Daniel Webster Highway, next to the state line

Mill-era and later housing

The Nashua Manufacturing Company was incorporated in 1823, and the mills ran until the last one near Nashua closed in 1949. The turnaround started with Sanders Associates, today part of BAE Systems, taking over a closed mill, and Digital Equipment Corporation arrived in the 1970s. The houses you see today come from both the mill era and the technology decades. Many buyers work in the Boston area and commute by the Everett Turnpike or the bus line from the Nashua Transit Center at Exit 8, so mention access when you describe a house.

Winter, snow and the roof

Winters in Nashua are real. Annual snowfall averages about 52.9 inches, precipitation 48.19 inches, and January's daily mean is 24.1 degrees Fahrenheit. Summers bring 26 to 30 days at 90 degrees or above. All that weather means the roof, gutters and basement are what you should check before listing, and what a cash buyer will price in.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Preparing a Nashua house for sale

Nashua buyers often arrive with a commute in mind, so be ready with details. Know where the property sits, whether downtown, French Hill, the Tree Streets, the Amherst Street corridor or South Nashua, because each has its own feel. Gather your last tax bill and the 8-digit parcel ID. Check how the roof, gutters and basement handled the last winter. If the house is a mill-era building, expect questions about wiring, plumbing and insulation.

Tell your title company early whether you have filed or plan to file an abatement. A decision either way can change the bill for your year of ownership, and that is simpler to settle before closing.

A cash sale lets you skip most of the repair list. The buyer builds condition into the offer, and you judge whether it beats what a repaired listing would net once commissions and months of carrying costs are subtracted.

Who handles property tax

At City Hall, 229 Main Street, Nashua, NH 03060, the Assessing Department sets values and the Tax Collector's Office bills and collects the tax.

OfficePhoneNotes
Assessing Department603-589-3040Abatement desk open Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., closed 12:30 to 1:30 p.m.
Tax Collector603-589-3190Mail to P.O. Box 885, Nashua, NH 03061

A payment in the mail is on time if the postmark carries the due date or earlier. Other options are the city's Pay Bills Online portal, the phone line at 1-833-343-0229, the counter, or the secure drop box at the Elm Street entrance of City Hall. Accepted payment forms include cash, major credit cards, checks, money orders and bank checks. Beginning with the first 2026 bills, taxpayers can see and download bills, payment history and balances online whenever they like.

Due dates and penalties

Two bills cover the April 1 to March 31 tax year. The first, due July 1, is an estimate at 50 percent of the prior year's rate. The second comes due once the state sets the rate, generally by December 20. When a home changes hands, tax is prorated by the day from April 1. Late payments pay 8 percent interest, matching RSA 76:13.

Recent rates per $1,000 of value show that a lower rate does not always mean a lower bill. The 2023 rate was $18.23. The 2024 rate was $15.90, down 12.8 percent, yet total value rose from $13.9 billion to $16.5 billion (18.7 percent). The 2025 rate was $16.83, up 5.83 percent. The city's Tax Rate History page has the figure that applies to your bill.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

How to file an abatement

Hand in a printed, signed application to the Assessing Department by March 1 after the notice of tax. The city takes applications only once the final notice of tax has been issued. Miss March 1 and the city can do nothing for that tax year, but you may ask for a spring review the next year.

The fillable online form cannot be submitted from the website. Print it, sign it and keep a copy, then deliver it to 229 Main Street or mail it to P.O. Box 2019, Nashua, NH 03061. Appeals past the city go to the New Hampshire Board of Tax and Land Appeals.

For a wrong name or address on the bill, send a signed written request from the owners by fax to 603-589-3079 or by mail to the Assessing Department. Only the Assessing Department can make that change.

If you sell and still get the bill

Pass the bill on to the new owner, or return it in the envelope provided with a note saying when you sold and to whom. Deeds take time to reach the Assessor, so a bill may arrive in the old owner's name.

Unpaid tax can become a lien under the state collection law. Under RSA 80:69, a recorded real estate tax lien accrues 14 percent interest a year, and the owner may redeem it until the collector issues a deed.

  • Closing agents can ask for a final wastewater bill through a form on the city's Tax and Wastewater page.
  • Look up an account with the 8-digit parcel ID in the upper right corner of the bill.
  • Each side pays the state transfer tax of $0.75 per $100 of price.

Questions to settle with the title company

Find out from the title company how it will prorate tax from April 1, whether a lien is recorded against the parcel, and how the final wastewater bill will be handled. Give it the 8-digit parcel ID and the date you expect to close. If you have an abatement application pending, tell the company in writing. Once you have closed, send along any bill that still shows up in your name. That way the new owner is not caught off guard while the city's records catch up with the deed.

These steps are small, but they prevent the common sources of delay: an unpaid balance, a missing parcel number, or a bill that went to the wrong address. Call the Tax Collector at 603-589-3190 for the balance, and the Assessing Department at 603-589-3040 for anything about your value.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

When are Nashua property tax bills due?

The first is due July 1. The second is generally due no later than December 20, once the state sets the rate.

What is the deadline to apply for a Nashua abatement?

By March 1 following the notice of tax. A missed deadline means no action that tax year, but you may request a spring review for the next year.

Are Nashua property taxes prorated when a house sells?

Yes. When a home is bought or sold, the city prorates tax by the day from April 1 of that year.

What interest does Nashua charge on late property tax?

8 percent. To avoid it, a mailed payment must carry a postmark on or before the due date.

Which county does Nashua's deed go to?

Hillsborough County. The deed is recorded with its Register of Deeds, where you also buy the transfer tax stamps at $0.75 per $100 from each side.

Cash Home Buyers in New Hampshire
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Concord, NH Property Tax Guide: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Concord, NH Property Tax Guide sale
  • Turn the Concord, NH Property Tax Guide offer down and you owe us nothing

Owe Concord Property Tax? Get a Cash Offer

We buy Concord houses as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Behind on Concord property tax?

Concord at a glance

Concord is New Hampshire's capital and the Merrimack County seat, roughly 16 miles north of Manchester and 66 miles north of Boston. Your tax depends on the city, the county and the school district, so start by finding out which part of Concord the house is in. The villages are Penacook, Concord Heights, East Concord and West Concord, and downtown has a North End and a South End.

Penacook falls in the Merrimack Valley School District instead of the Concord School District. Houses near the Merrimack River and its tributaries should be checked on the FEMA flood map. Winter tests roofs, heating systems and insulation each year, so a seller with an old furnace will hear about it from buyers.

Due dates and penalties

The city bills twice a year but collects in four installments. July and October are estimates, each 25 percent of the prior year's total bill. January and March are final and adjust for the earlier estimates.

InstallmentDue dateType
FirstJuly 1Estimate
SecondOctober 1Estimate
ThirdJanuary 2Final, adjusted
FourthMarch 31Final, adjusted

Expect the July and October bills together around June 1, and the January and March bills around December 1. They rest on the April 1 assessment under RSA 76:2. Late balances accrue 8 percent interest, prorated daily, under state law, and the city has no power to waive it.

Visit the Tax Collector at 41 Green Street or call 603-225-8540. The office opens Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday and Friday from 8:00 AM to 4:30 PM, and Thursday from 8:00 AM to 6:00 PM. Payment works online, by phone, in person, or by mail to the City of Concord Tax Office, PO Box 9582, Manchester, NH 03108. Mail it 7 to 10 days early.

Concord's tax rate

Concord charges $29.11 per $1,000 of assessed value for 2025, split as $10.18 for the city, $2.54 for the county, $1.58 for the state education tax and $14.81 for the local school district. The rate was set on November 19, 2025, on a valuation of $4,967,453,081 and a total commitment of $154,257,720.

Your own assessment decides your bill. The local school rate is the largest piece, and if your house is in Penacook or another part of the city, confirm your exact rate with the city assessor at 603-225-8550.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

The 2026 revaluation

Concord completed a citywide revaluation to bring assessments to full and true market value as of April 1, 2026. The state constitution says values must be set anew at least every five years, and the one before this was in 2021. New assessments are finalized before the final 2026 tax bill in December 2026, and abatement applications are available in the Assessing office after December 1, 2026.

  • Line up your new assessment against recent sales of similar houses.
  • If the number looks wrong, file an abatement application.
  • If you are selling, expect a buyer to underwrite the new value rather than your old one.

How to appeal your assessment

Apply to the city for an abatement by March 1 following the notice of tax. Under RSA 76:16, a person aggrieved by an assessment who has complied with RSA 74 may apply in writing by March 1, and the city must grant or deny in writing by July 1. A failure to respond counts as denial. For the current cycle the deadline is March 1, 2027.

If the city denies your request, the denial letter must explain the next appeal step. You can go to the Board of Tax and Land Appeals, phone 603-271-2578, or to superior court. The state sets the abatement form, so get the current one from the city or the Board.

If property tax goes unpaid

Unpaid tax can turn into a tax lien and eventually a tax deed, though the process takes at least two years. RSA 80:76 has the collector execute a deed to the lienholder two years after the lien if the land has not been redeemed. At least 30 days before that, the collector must notify the owner under RSA 80:77 and mortgage holders under RSA 80:77-a, by certified mail.

A sale that closes while the lien can still be redeemed clears it, since the title company pays the tax from your proceeds. Interest at 8 percent keeps adding to late balances, so a longer wait means a larger payoff.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Transfer tax when you sell

The state's real estate transfer tax is $0.75 per $100 of the price. Buyer and seller each owe it. Filing and payment happen online through Granite Tax Connect, and the Department of Revenue Administration answers questions at 603-230-5920. Who bears the cost in practice depends on your purchase and sale agreement, so read the closing costs line closely.

Selling a Concord house fast

Cash is the quickest route to a closing, while a listing can suit a house in good condition. A cash buyer takes the house as-is, which keeps a sale possible when there is deferred roof work, a tenant or a tax balance.

  • Request a payoff statement from your lender and a balance from the Tax Collector.
  • Look up your 2026 assessment and compare it with the old one.
  • Ask for a written offer and see who pays each closing cost.

We buy Concord houses as-is and do not charge commission or fees to the seller.

Tax proration and closing day

Concord's tax year is built on the April 1 assessment, and the four installments mean that on any closing date part of the year may already be paid and part may not. Ask the Tax Collector which installments have been paid on your parcel, and ask the title company how it will divide the year between you and the buyer. If your July or October payment was an estimate, remember that the January and March bills adjust for it, so the final figure can differ from what you paid earlier.

Bring the parcel information, the last bill and your lender's payoff statement to the first conversation with the title company. A seller who knows these numbers can read an offer line by line and see what actually lands in the bank.

The Assessing office at 603-225-8550 can tell you whether your 2026 value was set, and whether an abatement application is already on file for the parcel. A buyer's lender will look at the new value, not the old one, so be ready to talk about it.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

What buyers will notice in Concord

Concord's villages and neighborhoods shape what buyers expect. A house in Penacook, near Penacook Lake, is a different pitch from one in Concord Heights or the North End. Say which school district applies, mention whether the house is near the Merrimack or the Soucook, and keep your heating and roof records handy. If the 2026 assessment moved your value up or down, expect the buyer to ask about it in the first conversation.

If you own near the Soucook River, the Turkey River or the Contoocook, ask the city whether the flood map affects your parcel and keep the answer on file for the buyer.

Frequently asked questions

When are Concord property taxes due?

The four installments are due July 1, October 1, January 2 and March 31. July and October are estimates at 25 percent of last year's bill, and January and March are final adjusted payments.

What is the Concord tax rate?

The 2025 rate is $29.11 per $1,000: $10.18 city, $2.54 county, $1.58 state education and $14.81 local school.

What is the interest on late Concord property tax?

State law requires 8 percent interest, prorated daily, once a balance passes its due date. The city cannot waive it.

What is the abatement deadline in Concord?

Under RSA 76:16, applications are due by March 1 after the notice of tax. The deadline for the current cycle is March 1, 2027, and forms are available in Assessing after December 1, 2026.

Who pays the New Hampshire transfer tax?

Both of them. Each side pays $0.75 per $100 of the price, filed and paid online through Granite Tax Connect.
